title: Graceful output contraction and escape-resilience with idempotent resume tokens for streaming structured responses
creator: Maya Chen
description: Background: A growing set of customers use streaming structured JSON for tool/function calling and post-processing. When model responses are truncated mid-object or contain escaped payloads (e.g., user-supplied JSON blobs), downstream consumers either fail hard or invent heuristics that produce incorrect reconstructions. This ticket defines a formal contract and implementation plan for graceful 'contraction' (explicit, machine-readable markers that indicate omitted subtrees), escape-resilience strategies, and an idempotent resume token scheme to enable deterministic retries and safe reassembly across our API and SDKs.
acceptance_criteria: API can emit a compact contraction marker when truncation occurs that describes omitted keys, approximate byte counts, and a deterministic resume_token
SDKs (Python/Node) can resume a truncated stream using the resume_token and receive only the missing subtrees without duplicating previously received fields
Tool/function call boundaries are preserved: a tool call is never re-fired unless the resume point indicates it was not acknowledged by the tool endpoint
System handles nested escaped payloads (e.g., JSON strings inside fields) without double-unescaping or corruption
End-to-end tests simulate mid-object truncation, and all tests pass on CI with <1% false-negative reconstruction rate for synthetic corpora
technical_notes: Key constraints: resume_token must be deterministic (HMAC over request_id + model_state_anchor + byte_offset) to allow client-side verification and prevent replay ambiguity. Contraction markers should be small (<=256 bytes) and use a stable schema version. We must avoid changing the wire format for non-streaming clients. The runtime needs a small checkpoint hook to emit anchor points at safe boundaries (e.g., after top-level object fields or after tool call acknowledgements).
proposed_solution: 1) Define a lightweight contraction marker schema: {schema_version, missing_paths[], estimated_bytes, resume_token, safe_boundary}. 2) On truncation, append a final token in the stream (text/event or JSON chunk) that signals contraction. 3) Implement resume API: client provides resume_token and last_received_anchor, server replays only missing content and signals completion with a final 'contract-resolved' marker. 4) For tool calls, introduce an acknowledgement bit in the stream so the runtime will only retry tool invocations if acknowledgement was not seen prior to truncation. 5) SDKs will provide helper utilities to stitch contracted streams automatically and surface deterministic errors when reconstruction is impossible.
tradeoffs: - Pros: deterministic recovery, clearer client contracts, fewer silent corruption cases. - Cons: extra metadata increases response size slightly and adds complexity in runtime and SDKs. A bad resume_token design could leak information about internal model anchors; we use HMAC with ephemeral keys scoped to request to mitigate. There's added latency on resume flows (extra roundtrip) compared to naive retries.
test_plan: Unit tests for contraction marker generation/validation (HMAC tests, schema backward-compat)
Integration tests: run model generation simulator to force truncation at random byte offsets across nested JSON and escaped payloads
Tool-call invariants test: simulate tool endpoint side-effects and verify no duplicate tool calls after resume
SDK e2e: sample apps (chatbot + orchestration) consume truncated streams and stitch responses automatically
Load test: measure runtime CPU/memory impact of anchor checkpoints and resume flows at 99th percentile traffic
rollout_plan: Phase 1: runtime prototype behind a feature flag for internal customers + Python SDK alpha (canary). Phase 2: broader beta with Node SDK and Console observability flags showing truncation/resume events. Phase 3: default-on behavior after 4 weeks of beta and no high-severity issues. Rollback: disable feature flag at routing layer; SDKs continue to support older clients via compatibility shims.
